note: Read: on printed page 15 the report quotes Meeker ('says Meeker in Chicago, With Love. He continues:'), and the quotation runs on to printed page 16: 'There were Gothic wooden cottages...pleasant relics of a simpler day; Alt-Deutsch horrors with winged pigs on the roof; vaguely Venetian palazzi; ponderous constructions that seemed a far cry from the dignified Queen Anne or Georgian they aspired to.' The report's own words follow on page 16: 'The French style of architecture predominated, and so mansard and hipped roofs and dormer windows were de rigueur. Cupolas or towers were fairly common'. On printed page 22: 'William H. Murray, Arthur Meeker's maternal grandfather, who was a speculator on the Board of Trade, built the house at 1919 and soon sold it to his wife's brother, Charles Schwartz'; 'Schwartz, in turn, sold the house to Marshall Field when Marshall Jr. married in the early 1890s. This red-brick house, described by Meeker as "a rambling edifice...that has been rebuilt so often it's impossible to say any longer what it was originally trying to be," is still standing, currently occupied by a nursing home.' Not cited by any record yet: T-2642 read it to test a Queen Anne reading of 1919 Prairie, and the owner's ruling of 2026-10-19 left Queen Anne out of these scenes.
